newsitem.title: USA: New air traffic system nearly completed at Delhi.
newsitem.headline: New air traffic system nearly completed at Delhi.

text.p: A state-of-the-art air traffic control system was only months away from completion at the New Delhi airport when a mid-air collision on Tuesday resulted in some 350 deaths.
An antiquated air traffic control system was among the initial causes suspected for the disaster, but Indian aviation officials have since ruled that out as a reason for the crash.

The new system, awarded to Lexington, Mass.-based Raytheon in 1992 as part of a $92 million contract to upgrade the New Delhi and Bombay airports, has largely proceeded on schedule, company spokesman Barry French said.
The system includes primary and secondary radar systems which "allows very precise tracking of aircraft," he said.

"The automation system, which is the heart of an air traffic control system ... is state-of-the-art in that it provides information to air traffic controllers in a really easy to understand format and it eliminates confusion," French said.
The New Delhi system includes navigational aids, displays, air traffic control automation systems and detection radars.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration was consulting on the project as the radar systems were put through final site examination tests, French said. Most of the system has been installed but is not yet operational, he said.
